31: Hill explains that the secret is mentioned no fewer than a hundred times throughout the book but is never directly named, because it works more successfully when merely uncovered and left in sight for those who are READY and SEARCHING for it. This is why Carnegie tossed it so quietly without giving its specific name. Hill shares that his own son, while finishing his last year of college, picked up the Chapter 1 manuscript, discovered the secret, and used it so effectively that he went directly into a responsible position at a starting salary exceeding what the average person ever earns. Hill suggests this story may serve as an 'oasis in the Desert of Lost Hope' for readers who have been discouraged, faced difficulties, tried and failed, or been handicapped by illness or affliction. He also notes the secret was used extensively by President Woodrow Wilson during World War I, embedded in soldier training, and was a strong factor in raising war funds. Manuel L. Quezon, then Resident Commissioner of the Philippine Islands, was inspired by the secret to gain freedom for his people and became the first president of that free island nation. A peculiar characteristic: those who acquire and use the secret find themselves swept to success with apparent little effort and never again submit to failure.
32: Hill emphasizes a fundamental principle: 'There is no such thing as SOMETHING FOR NOTHING!' The secret cannot be had without a price, though the price is far less than its value. It cannot be purchased for money or given away because it comes in two parts—one part already being in possession of those ready for it. Education has nothing to do with it; Thomas A. Edison used the secret so intelligently he became the world's greatest inventor with only three months of schooling. The secret was also passed to an Edison business associate who, despite earning only $12,000 a year, accumulated a great fortune and retired young. Hill states that riches are not beyond any reader's reach. He then begins listing hundreds of well-known individuals who accumulated vast fortunes through the Carnegie secret, starting with: HENRY FORD, JOHN D. ROCKEFELLER, WILLIAM WRIGLEY JR., THOMAS A. EDISON, JOHN WANAMAKER, FRANK A. VANDERLIP, JAMES J. HILL, F. W. WOOLWORTH, FANNIE HURST, COL. ROBERT A. DOLLAR, GEORGE S. PARKER, EDWARD A. FILENE, E. M. STATLER, EDWIN C. BARNES, HENRY L. DOHERTY, ARTHUR BRISBANE, CYRUS H. K. CURTIS, and WOODROW WILSON.
33: The list of successful individuals continues: GEORGE EASTMAN, WILLIAM HOWARD TAFT, THEODORE ROOSEVELT, LUTHER BURBANK, JOHN W. DAVIS, EDWARD W. BOK, MARIE DRESSLER, FRANK A. MUNSEY, ELBERT HUBBARD, KATE SMITH, WILBUR WRIGHT, ELBERT H. GARY, WILLIAM JENNINGS BRYAN, ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL, DR. DAVID STARR JORDAN, JOHN H. PATTERSON, J. OGDEN ARMOUR, JULIUS ROSENWALD, CHARLES M. SCHWAB, STUART AUSTIN WIER, ERNESTINE SCHUMANN-HEINK, DR. FRANK CRANE, DR. FRANK GUNSAULUS, J.G. CHAPLINE, DANIEL WILLARD, ARTHUR NASH, KING GILLETTE, ELLA WHEELER WILCOX, RALPH A. WEEKS, CLARENCE DARROW, JUDGE DANIEL T. WRIGHT, and JENNINGS RANDOLPH. A footnote directs readers to endnotes beginning on page 313 for additional information about these individuals, many discussed on pages 316-322. Hill states these names represent but a small fraction of hundreds of Americans whose achievements prove that those who understand and apply the Carnegie secret reach high stations in life. He has never known anyone inspired to use the secret who did not achieve noteworthy success, nor anyone who achieved true distinction or accumulated significant riches without possessing the secret in some form. He concludes that the secret is more important for self-determination than anything received through 'education.' John Wanamaker told Hill his schooling was acquired like a steam locomotive takes on water—'by scooping it up as it runs.'
34: Hill notes that Henry Ford never reached high school, let alone college. He clarifies he is not minimizing formal education but expressing earnest belief that those who master and apply the secret will reach high stations, accumulate riches, and bargain with life on their own terms regardless of meager schooling. He tells readers that somewhere in the book, the secret will 'jump from the page and stand boldly before you IF YOU ARE READY FOR IT!' and when it appears, they should stop and celebrate, as that moment marks the most important turning point of their life. Hill transitions to the Introduction chapter, previewing the story of a dear friend who acknowledged seeing 'the mystic sign' and whose business achievements prove he discovered the secret. He reminds readers the book deals with facts, not fiction, and its purpose is to convey a great universal truth through which all who are READY may learn WHAT TO DO, HOW TO DO IT, and receive THE NEEDED STIMULUS TO MAKE A START. As a final clue, he offers: 'ALL ACHIEVEMENT, ALL EARNED RICHES, HAVE THEIR BEGINNING IN AN IDEA!' If ready, the reader already possesses one half of the secret and will recognize the other half the moment it reaches their mind. The preface is signed 'Napoleon Hill.'
35: This page features two contrasting inspirational maxims attributed to Napoleon Hill, separated by section marks. The first states: 'Success comes to those who become SUCCESS CONSCIOUS.' The second states: 'Failure comes to those who indifferently allow themselves to become FAILURE CONSCIOUS.' These two statements distill a core principle of Hill's philosophy: that success and failure are primarily determined by one's dominant mental orientation—conscious or unconscious—rather than by external circumstances. The concept of 'success consciousness' versus 'failure consciousness' recurs throughout the book as a foundational theme. The page serves as a motivational divider between the Author's Preface and the Introduction chapter.
36: This page opens the Introduction chapter, titled 'MINDPOWER: The Man Who Thought His Way.' Hill's opening declaration is: 'TRULY, THOUGHTS ARE THINGS—and powerful things at that when they are mixed with definiteness of purpose, persistence, and a BURNING DESIRE for their translation into riches or other material objects.' He introduces the story of Edwin C. Barnes, who discovered that individuals really can 'THINK AND GROW RICH.' Barnes' discovery came little by little, beginning with a BURNING DESIRE to become a business associate of the great Thomas Alva Edison. A key characteristic of Barnes' desire was its definiteness—he wanted to work WITH Edison, not FOR him. When the desire first flashed into Barnes' mind, two major obstacles stood in his way: he did not know Edison, and he lacked money for railroad fare to Orange, New Jersey. These difficulties would have discouraged most people, but Barnes' was no ordinary desire. He was so determined he decided to travel by 'blind baggage' (a freight train) rather than be defeated. He presented himself at Edison's laboratory and announced he had come to go into business with the inventor.
37: Edison later recalled Barnes standing before him 'looking like an ordinary tramp,' but sensing something in his facial expression that conveyed determination. Edison stated from years of experience: 'When a man really desires a thing so deeply that he is willing to stake his entire future on a single turn of the wheel in order to get it, he is sure to win.' Edison gave Barnes the opportunity because he saw Barnes had made up his mind to stand by until he succeeded. Hill emphasizes it was what Barnes THOUGHT that counted, not his appearance or words—Edison himself said so. Barnes did not get his partnership immediately; he got a chance to work in Edison's offices at nominal wages doing unimportant work that was nonetheless crucial because it gave him an opportunity to display his 'merchandise' where his intended partner could see it. Months passed with apparently nothing happening toward his goal, but something important was happening in Barnes' mind—he was constantly intensifying his DESIRE. Hill quotes psychologists: 'when one is truly ready for a thing, it puts in its appearance.' Barnes was ready and DETERMINED TO REMAIN READY UNTIL HE GOT THAT WHICH HE WAS SEEKING. He did not consider changing his goal; instead he declared: 'I came here to go into business with Edison, and I'll accomplish this end if it takes the remainder of my life.'
38: Hill reflects that Barnes' bulldog determination and persistence in standing behind a single DESIRE was destined to mow down all opposition. When opportunity came, it appeared in a different form and from a different direction than Barnes expected—one of the tricks of opportunity, which 'has a sly habit of slipping in by the back door, and it often comes disguised in the form of misfortune or temporary defeat.' This is why so many fail to recognize opportunity. Edison had just perfected the Edison Dictating Machine (later the Ediphone), but his sales staff were not enthusiastic and doubted it could be sold. Barnes saw his opportunity in this machine that interested no one but himself and the inventor. He suggested he could sell it, got his chance, and sold it so successfully that Edison gave him a contract to distribute and market it nationwide. The business alliance produced the slogan 'Made by Edison and Installed by Barnes' and lasted more than three decades. Barnes made himself rich in money, but more importantly, he proved that one really can 'Think and Grow Rich.' Hill estimates Barnes' original DESIRE may have brought him two or three million dollars, but the amount was insignificant compared to the definite knowledge he acquired: that an intangible impulse of thought can be 'transmuted' into its physical counterpart through known principles. Barnes literally thought himself into a fortune with nothing to start with except knowing what he wanted and the determination to stand by that desire until he realized it.
39: Hill summarizes Barnes' starting conditions: no money, little education, no influence—but he had initiative, faith, and the will to win, which made him 'number one man' with the greatest inventor who ever lived. Hill then transitions to a contrasting story: 'Three Feet from Gold,' about someone who had tangible evidence of riches but lost them by stopping three feet short of his goal. He states one of the most common causes of failure is quitting when overtaken by temporary defeat—every person is guilty of this at some point. An uncle of R. U. Darby caught 'gold fever' during the gold rush and went west to 'DIG AND GROW RICH.' Hill notes that more gold has been mined from the human brain than from the earth. Darby's uncle staked a claim, worked with pick and shovel, and after weeks of labor discovered shining ore. Needing machinery, he covered the mine, returned to Williamsburg, Maryland, and raised money from relatives and neighbors. The uncle and Darby returned to work the mine. The first car of ore proved they had one of the richest mines in Colorado—a few more cars would clear debts and produce huge profits. But then the vein of gold ore disappeared. They drilled desperately to pick up the vein again, all to no avail, and finally decided to QUIT. They sold the machinery to a junkman for a few hundred dollars and took the train home.
40: The junkman called in a mining engineer who calculated that the vein would be found JUST THREE FEET FROM WHERE THE DARBYS HAD STOPPED DRILLING—and that is exactly where it was found. The junkman took millions of dollars in ore from the mine because he sought expert counsel before giving up. R. U. Darby, who had helped procure the machinery money from relatives and neighbors, repaid every dollar though it took years. Darby later recouped his loss many times over in the life insurance business, applying the lesson: 'I stopped three feet from gold, but I will never stop because people say no when I ask them to buy insurance.' Darby became one of a small group (fewer than 50 individuals) who sold more than a million dollars of life insurance annually. Hill draws the moral: before success comes, every individual is sure to meet with temporary defeat and perhaps some failure. The easiest and most logical thing to do is QUIT, which is exactly what the majority do. More than 500 of the most successful individuals told Hill their greatest success came just one step beyond the point where defeat had overtaken them. 'Failure is a trickster with a keen sense of irony and cunning. It takes great delight in tripping one when success is almost within reach.' Hill then transitions to 'A 50-Cent Lesson in Persistence,' beginning another illustrative story.
